teaser: A canvas barely two feet wide, painted the year Mondrian found the language he would keep for life.
review_notes:
Dimensions given as about 59.5 x 59.5 cm: please confirm against the Kunstmuseum Den Haag record.
The yellow plane looks very pale (cream) in this reproduction; the lesson says so. Check against the real painting.
Claim that Mondrian painted flower pictures for income during the early 1920s in Paris.
Claim that the image shows the canvas without its frame, slightly cropped: line ends near the edges were read from this reproduction.

lesson.text: This painting is a square about 59.5 centimeters on each side, a little under two feet. You could carry it under one arm. It is oil paint on canvas, brushed by hand, with no ruler-perfect machine finish. Keep that modest size in mind, because the ideas packed into it are enormous.

Piet Mondrian was 49 when he painted it in Paris in 1921. He had spent thirty years getting here: first Dutch windmills and rivers, then trees that dissolved into branches, then grids of little dashes. Each step removed something. By 1921 only straight lines and flat rectangles were left.
Mondrian called his approach Neo-Plasticism, meaning “new image-making”: only horizontal and vertical lines, only red, yellow and blue, plus black, white and gray.

The title reads like a list of ingredients, and that is deliberate. No landscape, no person, no story. Notice which words come first, though: “Large Red Plane”. A plane is simply a flat area of color. The red one takes up almost a third of the canvas and sits in a corner, not in the middle.
To pay the rent in these years, the painter of pure rectangles kept producing delicate pictures of single flowers, chrysanthemums and lilies, which sold far more easily than his abstract canvases.

So how does a picture stay steady with all that red weight pushed up into one corner? Mondrian answers with smaller, quieter areas scattered on the other side. Follow the camera around the square and watch what each one does.

lesson.title: Weights and counterweights
lesson.text: Five kinds of area share this surface. Each one pulls on your eye with a different force.

spots.title: The red plane
spots.text: The loudest area by far. Its paint is not flat: faint vertical streaks from the brush run through it, so the red seems to breathe a little.

spots.title: The blue
spots.text: Small, saturated, and pushed to the opposite edge. Like a child on the far end of a seesaw, it balances a much bigger partner because it sits so far away.

spots.title: A black plane
spots.text: Black is used here as a color in its own right, filling a rectangle. A second black area sits above the blue on the right. In later years he kept black mostly for lines.

spots.title: The yellow
spots.text: In this reproduction it is a pale, creamy yellow, almost a whisper. It anchors the bottom without competing with the red.

lesson.text: Did you see that the “white” areas were not white? The title says gray, and it means it. The pale rectangles are tinted with a cool bluish gray. Pure white next to that red would have glared. These grays let the eye rest, the way silence works between notes.

Mondrian believed that everything in nature, under its changing surface, comes down to a play of opposites: upright and lying down, active and calm, color and no color. A painting made only of those opposites, held in balance, could show a harmony that a picture of a tree or a face would hide.
He was born Pieter Mondriaan, with two a's. Around the time he first moved to Paris he dropped one of them, a small edit that made the name feel less Dutch and more international.

The black lines look like a rigid cage. They are not. Several of them were painted so that they quit just before reaching the edge of the canvas, leaving a sliver of gray. One on the left side is the easiest to catch.
One black line on the left stops in mid-air, well before the edge of the canvas. Tap its free end.

spots.title: The line that stops
spots.text: This horizontal bar ends a finger's width from the left edge. The gray plane flows around its tip, so the grid feels painted and open, not like a window frame nailed shut.

lesson.text: That little gap changes how the whole thing reads. A line that touches the edge suggests the grid continues beyond the canvas. A line that stops short reminds you that someone decided, by hand, exactly where it should end. In 1921 Mondrian was still testing both options from picture to picture.

At the very bottom, near the middle, he tucked his initials and the year: PM 21. He had helped launch a magazine called De Stijl, Dutch for “The Style”, in 1917, and architects and furniture makers in its circle were already applying the same lines and colors to chairs and houses.
The balance here is asymmetric: nothing mirrors anything else, yet nothing tips over. A big color in a corner can be held by a small one far away.

quiz.question: Roughly how big is this painting?
options: About 60 cm (2 ft) on each side
About 2 meters (6.5 ft) on each side
quiz.explanation: It is a square of about 59.5 cm, a little under two feet.

quiz.question: What does “plane” mean in the title?
quiz.explanation: A plane is simply a flat area of color.

quiz.question: What are the pale rectangles actually painted in?
quiz.explanation: The title says gray, and the pale areas are tinted with a cool gray.

quiz.question: What does the small blue rectangle do in the composition?
options: It balances the large red plane from the far edge
quiz.explanation: A small saturated color far away can balance a much bigger one.

quiz.question: What does Neo-Plasticism allow?
options: Only horizontal and vertical lines and primary colors with black, white and gray
Any color as long as lines are diagonal
quiz.explanation: Mondrian limited himself to straight horizontals and verticals, primaries, black, white and gray.

facts.text: Every black line in this painting runs all the way to the edge of the canvas.
facts.explanation: Several stop short, like the horizontal bar on the left.

facts.text: While painting works like this, Mondrian also sold flower pictures to earn a living.
facts.explanation: Flowers sold far more easily than his abstract canvases.

facts.text: The large red plane sits exactly in the middle of the canvas.
facts.explanation: It is pushed into the upper left corner.
